newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Yacht search suspended, rescues at the limit.
newsitem.headline: Yacht search suspended, rescues at the limit.

text.p: Last week's Australian sea rescues reached virtually the limit that could be accomplished with even the best equipment, Australian authorities said as a search for another yacht race competitor was suspended.
"It was almost the limit of what could be achieved," Mike Calway, one of Australia's senior search co-ordinators, said of the rescue of two race competitors 2,600 km (1,600 miles) towards Antarctica.

Calway said Frenchman Thierry Dubois and Briton Tony Bullimore, whose yachts capsized, had been in almost the worst possible combination of circumstances: great distance from land, foul weather and remoteness from merchant shipping routes.

But Canadian Gerry Roufs is lost in an even more remote area between New Zealand, South America and Antarctica and France-3 television said a cargo ship and another competitor looking for him had given up the search.
Another ship is heading for the area, however.

Even Australia's Orion maritime aircraft, designed for long-endurance submarine hunting, used almost all their fuel getting to and from Dubois and Bullimore, leaving just two or three hours for searching and watching over the yachtsmen.

Orion navigator David Jeffcoat said the aircraft had to rely on their extensive sensor suite -- two radars, a heat-detecting infrared camera, listening sonar buoys and binoculars stabilised against bumps in flight -- to find and communicate with the yachtsmen.
Calway said the yachts' advanced distress beacons, which gave more accurate positions than old models, had also been an important part of the technology that saved the yachtsmen.
Two Orions found Dubois and Bullimore's boat on Monday, although it was four days before Bullimore was discovered alive inside.
But Roufs is lost in an area 4,200 km (2,600 miles) from land -- beyond effective aircraft radius.

Even though they were just within air-search range, Dubois and Bullimore were still in trouble after they were found, because only a ship could pluck them from the sea, and merchant ships rarely venture so close to Antarctica.
So the Perth-based frigate HMAS Adelaide had to beat its way through rough weather at best speed for 2-1/2 days to reach them.

And even that was barely possible, because the long dash at high power used up almost all of the Adelaide's fuel. The Australian navy has had to send a tanker to refuel the frigate on its way back to Perth, where it should dock on Monday.
"Bullimore is sleeping better than I thought he would," the Adelaide's captain, Raydon Gates, told the Australian Associated Press on Sunday.
"At this stage he could be expecting nightmares, continuing to re-live the event, become more inward-looking, almost withdrawn.

"In fact he's going the other way. He's coming out, he's quite keen to retain company and be with people. He's obviously quite a gregarious man in himself and a lot of this (spirit) has not been dampened."
The Australian government said on Saturday that Bullimore would have to go into hospital on arrival.
Bullimore's wife left London on Saturday to meet him in Perth.
The Australian air force rescued another competitor in the same French-organised race, the Vendee Globe Challenge, on December 27.
On that occasion an Orion found Frenchman Raphael Dinelli and dropped a life raft a few minutes before his yacht sank.
